title: The Sacred Atlas
subtitle: Every sacred site on Earth that depicts or worships a being with a PuniCodex temple — plotted, dated, and linked to its digital twin.
note: Coordinates are approximate monument centers. Deity identifications follow mainstream scholarship (UNESCO nominations, museum records, Assyriological and classical scholarship); contested or restricted identifications say so openly. Wikimedia Commons imagery is curated separately through the gallery curator and lands in each site's images array.

sites.name: Giza Pyramid Complex

deities.depiction: The king is buried as Osiris and rises as Ra — the Pyramid Texts, the world's oldest religious corpus, line the walls of Unas' pyramid.
The living king is Horus; the pyramid is his staircase to join the sun's circuit.

sources: Pyramid Texts of Unas, c. 2350 BCE

deities.depiction: Ramses II enthroned between the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty and Amun-Ra on the facade; the temple axis was engineered so sunlight reaches the sanctuary on the king's birthday.
Ra-Horakhty — Ra as the Horus of the horizon — anchors the facade colossi.

sites.name: Karnak Temple Complex
sites.era: c. 2055 BCE – 100 CE, built over 2,000 years

deities.depiction: The Amun precinct — the largest religious complex ever built, grown by every dynasty for two millennia.
Amun-Ra: the hidden one becomes the visible sun; the Great Hypostyle Hall is his forest.

sources: Centre Franco-Égyptien d'Étude des Temples de Karnak

deities.depiction: The temple of the Opet festival, where Amun's barque procession renewed the king and the flood alike.
Every royal tomb is a machine for becoming Osiris: the Book of the Dead and Amduat maps of the underworld line the burial chambers.
The Temple of Ḥwt-ḥr, Lady of the Sycamore — the best-preserved temple ceiling in Egypt, blue with Nut's body and the decans.

sites.name: Temple of Edfu

deities.depiction: The House of Horus — the best-preserved temple in Egypt, where Horus of Behdet triumphed over Seth in the annual drama of the walls.

sources: Edfu Project, Akademie der Wissenschaften, Göttingen

deities.depiction: The last temple of ancient Egypt, where Isis' cult outlived the empire and was still honoured in the 6th century CE; moved stone by stone above the flood.
The moon god Nanna's mountain — Ur's ziggurat, rebuilt by Saddam Hussein and conserved again after 2003.
Nebuchadnezzar's processional way — glazed lions of Ishtar pacing toward her city's festivals.
The Eanna — 'House of Heaven' — Inanna's precinct at the world's first city, where writing itself was born in her temple's accounts.
Inanna is Ištar's Sumerian name — one goddess, two languages.
The Abzu — Enki/Ea's temple over the subterranean fresh-water deep. Sumerian tradition names Eridu's shrine the FIRST temple ever founded.
The tablets of the Gilgameš epic slept here for two and a half millennia until Layard's dig — the first hero's afterlife began in this library.
The Ishtar temple of Nineveh stood beside the North Palace.
Athena Parthenos — Phidias' thirty-foot gold and ivory statue stood where the treasury of an empire funded a goddess' house.
The omphalos — the navel of the world — and the Pythia's tripod, where Apollo spoke through the priestess.
The temple of Apóllōn, slayer of the Python; his oracle shaped the politics of the Greek world for a thousand years.
Phidias' chryselephantine Zeus — seated, smiling, one of the Seven Wonders of the World; the games honoured him every four years.
The island of Apollo's birth — Leto delivered him here beneath the palm, and the whole island became his sanctuary, treasury and free port.
The healing god's hospital-sanctuary — incubation halls, the snake, and a theatre with acoustics engineers still cite.
The citadel whose Linear B tablets first write the name of Zeus — a god three centuries older than Homer.

sites.name: Knossos

deities.depiction: The labyrinth's thread — the Ariadne whose ball of string tamed the Minotaur's maze beneath this palace.

sources: Arthur Evans excavations; Linear A/B archives

deities.depiction: The temple of all gods — its dome the vault of heaven, its oculus the sun itself; every god Rome met had a place in the sphere.
The Capitolium — Jupiter Optimus Maximus' temple that gave every capital city its name.
An Egyptian goddess in a Roman town — frescoed days before Vesuvius fell, showing Isis' cult as everyday Mediterranean religion.
Baal of the Bekaa — the city kept its Canaanite storm god's name through three religions.
Rome's trilithon colossus: Jupiter Heliopolitanus, with Bacchus and Venus completing the triad.

sites.name: Jelling — The Conversion Stones
sites.deityNote: Harald Bluetooth's runestones — Denmark's baptism certificate. The pagan gods are notably absent: that absence is the monument's whole point.

deities.depiction: Adam of Bremen (c. 1070) describes the temple: Thor enthroned centrally, flanked by Wodan and Fricco.
Wodan — Óðinn — with his warriors and birds.
Fricco — Freyr — with his priapus and peace; the great burial mounds stand beside the site.
The longest runic inscription in stone — eight hundred years of scholarship later, its riddles still argue about Óðinn and the dead.
Older than Stonehenge and the pyramids; later Irish myth made the great mound the síd of the Dagda, lord of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
The Hill of Kings — where Lugh's harvest games were played and Ireland's kings were inaugurated with the marriage of the land.

sites.name: Avebury
sites.deityNote: A Neolithic henge older than any named god in this lexicon — the largest stone circle in Europe, its cult unnamed and unrecovered.
sources: UNESCO WHL 373 (Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites)

sites.name: Stonehenge
sites.deityNote: Built in stages over fifteen centuries. Every named deity attached to it in modern folklore is projection — the builders' gods are lost.

deities.depiction: A mountain carved top-down out of a single basalt cliff — Śiva's home in the real world. The plinth carries the Rāvaṇa shaking-Kailāsa relief; shrine niches across the walls hold the whole pantheon.
The Trimūrti — three faces of the Great Lord — carved into the island's basalt; Śiva as creator, preserver and destroyer in one six-metre head.
The Kandariya Mahadeo — Śiva's marble mountain, its shikhara carved with eight hundred figures rising to the sky.
The largest religious monument on Earth — built as Viṣṇu's temple, its galleries a four-kilometre relief of the Churning of the Sea of Milk.
The Chola colossus — a vimana of granite crowned with a single eighty-tonne capstone, Śiva's house built to outlast the dynasty.
Kāśī — the city founded to Śiva, where the ghats have burned with funeral fires for three thousand years without interruption.
The island where Rāma worshipped Śiva before crossing to Laṅkā — the epic's bridge begins here.
Meenakshi — the fish-eyed goddess, a royal form of Pārvatī, who ruled Madurai and married Śiva in the temple's annual grand wedding.
The Sun's chariot of stone — twelve carved wheels, seven straining horses, Sūrya rising over the Bay of Bengal.
A mandala you climb — two million blocks, ten terraces, and at the summit the great stupa; the central Buddha's identity is debated, with Mahāvairocana the leading reading.
The Great Stupa — Ashoka raised it over the Buddha's relics; its toranas narrate the life in stone.
The diamond throne beneath the Bodhi tree — the exact ground of the awakening, the holiest site in Buddhism.

sites.name: Tōdai-ji, Nara

deities.depiction: The Daibutsu — Mahāvairocana in gilded bronze, the largest bronze Buddha ever cast when Emperor Shōmu raised it.

sources: Shōsōin documents; UNESCO WHL 870 (Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara)

deities.depiction: Amitābha in the open air — the hall that housed him was swept away by a tsunami in 1498, and the Buddha has sat outdoors ever since.

sites.name: Ise Jingū

deities.depiction: The shrine of the Sun Goddess — Amaterasu's mirror is one of the Three Treasures of the throne; the Shikinen Sengū renewal has kept carpenters in unbroken practice for thirteen centuries.

sources: Ise Shō Naike tradition; UNESCO (tentative list)

deities.depiction: Ten thousand vermilion torii climbing the mountain — the kami of rice, sake and success, foxes at every gate.
The great torii standing in the tide — the shrine honours the three daughters of Susanō, the storm god.
The great shrine of Ōkuninushi, lord of the land who yielded it to Amaterasu's line in exchange for the shrine's rank — Japan's oldest recorded diplomatic settlement.

sites.name: Kasuga Taisha
sites.deityNote: The four clan kami of the Fujiwara ride here in annual procession; the Fujiwara kami are not yet in the lexicon.
sources: UNESCO WHL 870 (Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara)

sites.name: Temple of Heaven
sites.deityNote: The altar of Tiān — Heaven itself, unrepresented as image; the Son of Heaven prayed here for the harvest. The high god Di 帝, named on Shang oracle bones, is the deep ancestor of this rite.

deities.depiction: The headquarters of the Complete Perfection order, where Lǎozī is honoured as Taishang Laojun — the Lord Lao Most High.
The Peak that Flew from Afar — its cliffs carry Song-dynasty carvings of Guānyīn among the largest surviving stone bodhisattvas in China.
The Perfected Warrior's mountain — Zhenwu, the dark lord of the north, subdued his serpent and tortoise here; the Ming emperor built the Golden Hall in his honour.

sites.name: Mount Qingcheng

deities.depiction: The mist mountain where the Way of the Celestial Masters began — organized Taoism's birthplace in the shadow of Dujiangyan's waters.

sources: UNESCO WHL 1001 (Mount Qingcheng and the Dujiangyan Irrigation System)

deities.depiction: Royal tombs cut into the cliff — every investiture scene shows the winged symbol of Ahura Mazdā hovering over the king; a fire altar burns below.
Every foundation inscription opens the same way — 'by the favour of Ahura Mazdā'. The apadana's tribute bearers walked past the faravahar of the Wise Lord.
A sacred fire kept burning for centuries — the physical custody of the Wise Lord's truth.

sites.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)

deities.depiction: The tablets of the Baal Cycle — the storm god's battle with Prince Sea was read here until the city burned.
The high god's marzeah — El, Father of Years, enthroned at the source of the rivers.
ꜥAnat's furious war-poem fills the gaps of the cycle; she waded in blood up to the knees.

sources: RS 3.322+ tablets; editio princeps by Virolleaud

deities.depiction: The Lady of Byblos — Baalat Gebal, the city's mistress, kin to Astarte; her temple endured through five millennia of rebuilds.

sites.name: Carthage Tophet

deities.depiction: The precinct of Tanit and Baal Hammon — thousands of stelae to the Lady of Carthage; Tanit is not yet in the lexicon, Astarte's Punic daughter stands here.

sources: American Schools of Oriental Research excavations

sites.name: Tel Megiddo
sites.deityNote: Twenty-six layers of cult and war — Armageddon's tel. Canaanite temples stood here; the specific dedications are lost in the strata.

deities.depiction: The rock galleries' procession of gods — the Hittite pantheon carved in basalt relief, marching toward the storm god's embrace.
The sword-god of Chamber B — the Hittite storm god with his hieroglyphic name.
The storm god of Ḫatti's great temple in the Hittite capital, beside the archives that held 30,000 cuneiform tablets.

sites.name: Alaca Höyük
sites.deityNote: Hattian royal tombs at the sacred spring — the stratum beneath the Hittite stratum, before the Indo-European names arrived.

deities.depiction: The Perun shrine of Novgorod — Vladimir's pantheon head before baptism; the idols were thrown down here in 988.

sites.name: Arkona — Cape Arkona
sites.deityNote: Svantevit's temple-fortress stood on this cape until the Danes razed it in 1168, carrying the idol's head to Lund. Svantevit is not yet in the lexicon.

deities.depiction: Ọṣun's living grove on the river — shrines, sculptures and the goddess's annual festival, unbroken and UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Ile-Ife

deities.depiction: The cradle city of the Yoruba — Odùduwà descended here and founded the line of kings; the naturalistic bronzes of Ife are among humanity's finest portrait sculpture.

sources: Ife corpus bronzes; British Museum/Ife Museum

sites.name: Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan

deities.depiction: The double temple's north half — Tlāloc's altar with its blue-and-white paint still bright when Cortés arrived.
The south half — Huītzilōpōchtli's shrine, the hummingbird of war, rebuilt five times as the empire grew.

sources: UNESCO WHL 412 (Historic Centre of Mexico City)

deities.depiction: The Feathered Serpent's pyramid — two hundred sacrificed warriors cemented its foundations six hundred years before the Aztec named the city 'the place where the gods were born'.
The largest pyramid on Earth by volume — Aztec legend held this was Quetzalcōātl's city before his departure east over the sea.
The golden enclosure of the Sun — walls sheeted in gold that the conquistadors stripped within a year; the Dominican church stands inside its perfect masonry now.
The Intihuatana — the hitching-post of the sun, where the priests tied the sun to the stone at solstice so it could not wander off.

sites.name: Sacsayhuamán
sites.deityNote: The thunderhead fortress above Cuzco — walls of stones fitted without mortar, the storm's seat above the city of the Sun.

deities.depiction: The only great temple of Wiraqucha — the creator's house at the centre of the Inca road, its central wall two metres thick and forty metres long.
The city of refuge — under Lono's law of sanctuary, anyone who reached these walls was absolved, whatever their crime.

sites.name: Taputapuātea
sites.deityNote: The marae that anchored the voyaging triangle — canoes were dedicated here before the long passages. ʻOro, its war god, is not yet in the lexicon; Taʻaroa of the deep is Tangaroa.

sites.name: Mauna Kea
sites.deityNote: Mauna a Wākea — the mountain of the sky father, where the umbilical cord of the islands was buried. Wākea is not yet in the lexicon.
sources: Hawaiian traditional knowledge; DLNR conservation records

deities.depiction: The quarry where the moai were born — under Makemake, the creator who made humanity from a bird-man's egg at Orongo.

sites.name: Uluru
sites.deityNote: Sacred to the Aṉangu. The specific beings of its stories are restricted men's and women's knowledge, not ours to publish — this atlas honours the restriction.

sites.name: Ubirr Rock Art
sites.deityNote: Forty thousand years of painting in one gallery — the Rainbow Serpent's oldest images live here; the Rainbow Serpent is not yet in the lexicon.

sites.name: Budj Bim Cultural Landscape
sites.deityNote: The oldest aquaculture on Earth — Gunditjmara-engineered eel channels older than the pyramids, still in the story of the landscape serpent.

deities.depiction: The shrine of the three — Hwanin of heaven, Hwanung of the mountain, and Dangun, the bear-son who founded Korea.
The granite grotto facing the sea — Śākyamuni touches the earth in the pose of the awakening, encircled by bodhisattvas carved from a single granite dome.

sites.name: Jongmyo Shrine
sites.deityNote: The royal ancestral shrine — Korea's kings honoured as spirits, the oldest Confucian royal rite still performed.

sites.name: Cerro Ñielol
sites.deityNote: The sacred hill at the heart of Mapuche Temuco — treaty-signed ground beneath native forest, still honoured.
sources: Corporación Cerro Ñielol; Treaty of Tapihue site tradition

sites.name: Villarrica Volcano
sites.deityNote: Ruka Pillán — 'the house of the Pillán', the thunder spirits. The Mapuche name is older than the Spanish volcano.

deities.depiction: The last pagan capital's sacred groves — Lithuania kept its oaks and its thunder god until 1387, and Kernavė's hillforts remember.
The mountain of the gods — Mytikas at 2,917 m was the first Greek peak climbed for its own myth; the gods' city was always above the weather, which is why no one found it.
